name: Selective Annotation Makes Language Models Better Few-Shot Learners (vote-k)
venue: ICLR 2023 (Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations); preprint arXiv:2209.01975 (submitted 5 Sep 2022). DBLP key conf/iclr/SuKWSWX0OZS023 confirms acceptance at ICLR 2023.
authors_affiliation: Hongjin Su, Jungo Kasai, Chen Henry Wu, Weijia Shi, Tianlu Wang, Jiayi Xin, Rui Zhang, Mari Ostendorf, Luke Zettlemoyer, Noah A. Smith, Tao Yu. Affiliations: The University of Hong Kong (Su, Yu); University of Washington (Kasai, Shi, Zettlemoyer, Smith, Ostendorf); Allen Institute for AI; Carnegie Mellon University (Wu); Penn State University (Zhang); Meta AI (Wang). Corresponding/lead: Hongjin Su and Tao Yu (HKU).
maintained_repo_url: N/A (single-paper author/lab repo; no continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).
task_domain: In-context learning / few-shot demonstration (prompt) retrieval for diverse NLP tasks, with a focus on annotation efficiency. Tasks span classification (paraphrase, sentiment, topic, NLI), commonsense reasoning (multiple-choice), dialogue state tracking, and text/code generation (semantic parsing, open-domain QA, summarization). QA-adjacent; not an agent/tool/embodied setting.
problem_setting: Offline, supervised-budget, single-model (no multi-agent) setting. Departing from prior ICL work that assumes a large fully-annotated training set is available for prompt retrieval, the paper formulates a two-step annotation-efficient framework: (1) selective annotation - before test time, choose a small subset L (size = annotation budget M, e.g. M=18 or 100) from an unlabeled pool X to annotate; (2) prompt retrieval - at test time, retrieve similar in-context examples from the annotated pool L for each test instance. The vote-k selection method itself is UNSUPERVISED (uses Sentence-BERT embeddings plus the inference LM's own prediction confidence on unlabeled data; no labels needed during selection). Supervision enters only when the selected pool is then annotated. The inference LM is frozen (no parameter updates). Selection is deterministic given a fixed unlabeled pool; variance is simulated by subsampling 3K unlabeled instances three times. Two regimes by budget: M=18 (all fit in context, no retrieval step) vs M=100 (similarity-based prompt retrieval at test time).
what_is_retrieved: Demonstrations (annotated input-output training examples) used as in-context prompts. At test time, similar annotated examples are retrieved from the selectively-annotated pool L. (The upstream 'selective annotation' step is itself a selection/coreset procedure that builds the pool, not a per-instance retrieval.)
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: the fixed selectively-annotated pool L is the retrieval store. It is built offline once (via vote-k selection + annotation) and frozen; it is not a growing/episodic agent memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Two-stage objective. (a) Selective annotation optimizes COVERAGE/representativeness-plus-diversity of the annotated pool (a set-coverage-style goal: pick a diverse, representative subset so many future test instances find a similar demonstration) rather than a fixed top-k ranking. (b) Prompt retrieval at test time is similarity-style top-k ranking (most-similar examples by cosine similarity), with k effectively budget-capped (fill the LM context). It is not framed as recovering a minimal complete tool/demo set.
cbr_cycle_coverage: Retrieve (yes, similarity-based prompt retrieval from the annotated pool) / Reuse (yes, retrieved demonstrations injected verbatim as in-context exemplars) / Revise (no) / Retain (no). Effectively [Retrieve, Reuse]. The distinctive contribution is the upstream construction of the case base (which cases to annotate), not the CBR adaptation loop.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the work frames itself as in-context learning with selective annotation + prompt retrieval; it does not present itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is conceptually adjacent (building a small high-quality case base for reuse) but not explicitly CBR-grounded.
retrieval_unit: Single demonstration (one annotated training input-output pair / example), e.g. an utterance-label pair, a multiple-choice context-continuation, a dialogue-state pair, or an utterance-SQL pair. Granularity = single demo / case (problem-solution).
index_source: Static corpus, offline-induced. The retrievable store is the selectively-annotated pool L, built offline by the unsupervised graph-based vote-k method (Sentence-BERT embeddings + LM confidence over an unlabeled pool) and then annotated. No online/test-time growth. The unlabeled pool itself is subsampled (3K) from the original training data.
index_structure_topology: Two layers. (1) Selection-time: a directed k-nearest-neighbor GRAPH G=(V,E) over Sentence-BERT embeddings of unlabeled instances (each vertex connects to its k=150 nearest neighbors by cosine similarity), used by the vote-k scoring. (2) Retrieval-time: a flat dense embedding store over the annotated pool L (Sentence-BERT embeddings, cosine-similarity nearest-neighbor lookup). So selection uses a kNN graph; test-time retrieval uses a flat vector index.
retriever_type: Off-the-shelf dense / similarity retriever (no learned/trained retriever). Sentence-BERT (all-mpnet-base-v2, averaged token embeddings) is used both to build the selection graph and to compute test-time cosine-similarity nearest neighbors. The novelty is in the SELECTION objective (vote-k graph algorithm), not in a learned retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: None / off-the-shelf for the retriever itself (frozen Sentence-BERT cosine similarity; no contrastive or RL training of a retriever). However, the SELECTION step uses an unsupervised graph degree score combined with the inference LM's own confidence (average log-probability of the LM's generation over unlabeled instances) to pick diverse, representative examples - i.e. selection is LM-confidence-informed but not a trained retriever and not label-supervised. 'Fast vote-k' drops the LM-confidence component entirely (pure graph score).
query_construction: At test time the raw test input is encoded by Sentence-BERT to form the query (no decomposition/expansion/intent-extraction); nearest annotated examples by cosine similarity are retrieved. No query rewriting.
query_granularity: Task-level / instance-level, one-shot at t=0: a single query is formed once per test instance; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying. (When M=18 there is no per-instance query at all - the same 18 selected examples are fixed in the prompt for every test instance.)
when_to_retrieve: One-shot: retrieval happens once per test instance before generation (only in the M=100 / large-pool regime). In the M=18 regime there is no test-time retrieval - the fixed annotated pool is used directly as the prompt. No iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule (retrieve once per test instance, unconditionally, before LM decoding, when a retrieval step is used). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger at test time. (LM confidence is used only at offline selection time, not as a test-time retrieval trigger.)
reranking: No dedicated reranking stage. Retrieved annotated examples are simply ordered by cosine similarity. (At selection time there is an iterative confidence-bucketing procedure, but that builds the pool, not a test-time rerank.)
retrieved_context_refinement: None beyond similarity ordering and context-budget truncation. As many retrieved examples as fit in the LM's maximum token length are kept (on average 13.4 in-context examples across experiments), concatenated in ASCENDING order of similarity so the most similar example is nearest the test input (exploiting recency bias, Lu et al. 2022). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (no tools/skills; retrieved units are raw annotated demonstrations).
index_content_separation: N/A / No: the full demonstration text is both indexed (via Sentence-BERT embedding) and loaded into the prompt; no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure split.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A (no tool index or live protocol; static dense store over a fixed annotated pool).
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation: retrieved (or, at M=18, fixed selected) annotated examples are concatenated as in-context demonstrations before the test input and fed to the frozen inference LM. For classification/multiple-choice the LM scores each candidate label (max average log-probability); for generation it does beam-search decoding. No parameter updates; verbatim exemplar use.
planning_integration: One-shot exemplars at inference time (select-then-annotate offline, then retrieve-then-generate). Not interleaved with planning/search; a single retrieval (or fixed prompt) feeds a single decode. No MCTS/tree-search/hierarchical integration.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-answer / per-instance: a single retrieval (or fixed prompt) feeds one decode of the full output; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-token.
adaptation_mechanism: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved/selected demonstrations are used as-is in the prompt; no explicit case adaptation/revision step.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw demonstration text: the surface form of each retrieved unit is the concatenation of the annotated example's input and gold output (a raw problem-solution pair), injected directly into the prompt. No distillation into strategies/workflows.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Single demonstration (raw, un-distilled annotated example / problem-solution pair); not a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Stability and outlier-robustness come from the SELECTION design plus similarity retrieval rather than a test-time relevance filter. Vote-k jointly optimizes diversity + representativeness, reducing variance across unlabeled-data subsamples; the paper argues similarity-based prompt retrieval is robust to outliers/small annotation sizes because each test instance retrieves only its most similar examples (evidenced by the random-prompt-retrieval ablation in 4.4 and the outlier-removal finetuning analysis in Appendix E/Table 9). No learned relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware SFT.
memory_type: none (static selectively-annotated pool; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
write_back: False: the system does not store new experiences/cases into memory during deployment; the annotated pool is fixed after offline selection + annotation.
online_growth: No: the annotated pool / index is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow at test time.
write_back_trigger: never (no write-back; the annotated pool is static after offline selection).
failure_experience_usage: Not used as deployment memory. The selection procedure uses the inference LM's confidence (average log-probability) over unlabeled instances to bucket and diversify the pool, but it does not store labeled failures/negatives as a contrastive memory; selection is unsupervised and there is no success/failure trajectory store.
memory_evolution_update: N/A / append-only-none: the annotated pool is built once and never mutated after annotation.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: neither selection nor retrieval is an RL/value-based learned policy. Selection is a deterministic graph + LM-confidence heuristic (vote-k); test-time retrieval is fixed top-k by off-the-shelf Sentence-BERT cosine similarity.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-model, single private annotated pool / retriever. (Cross-LM transfer is studied descriptively - the same selected pool is evaluated with GPT-Neo 2.7B, GPT-J 6B, GPT-3 175B, OPT-175B, Codex - but there is no shared multi-agent memory.)
benchmarks: 10 datasets across 9 tasks: MRPC (paraphrase detection), SST-5 (sentiment), DBpedia (topic classification), MNLI (NLI), RTE (NLI), HellaSwag (commonsense multiple-choice), MWoZ 2.4 (dialogue state tracking), GeoQuery (semantic parsing / text-to-SQL), NQ / Natural Questions (open-domain QA), XSUM (summarization). Domain-shift analysis adds two WILDS datasets: CivilComments (toxicity) and Amazon (review classification), each with random vs domain splits.
benchmark_family: Primarily classic NLP/QA: classification + NLI (GLUE-style: MRPC, MNLI, RTE, SST-5, DBpedia), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag), dialogue (MWoZ), semantic parsing/code (GeoQuery), open-domain QA (NQ), summarization (XSUM), plus distribution-shift (WILDS: CivilComments, Amazon). Not in the agent/web/embodied/tool benchmark families; closest normalized grouping is QA + classification/NLI (GLUE) with some structured generation.
baselines: (1) Selective-annotation baselines (the core comparison): RANDOM selection (averaged over 3 trials), Maximizing Facility Location (MFL; Lin & Bilmes 2009, submodular greedy, representativeness), Diversity (max embedding diversity), Least-confidence (Lewis & Gale 1994, active learning), and Fast vote-k (vote-k without the LM-confidence step). (2) Prompt-retrieval baseline: Random prompt retrieval vs similarity-based retrieval (Liu et al. 2022). (3) Paradigm baseline: supervised finetuning of strong PLMs - RoBERTa-large for MRPC and HellaSwag, DS2-T5 (Shin et al. 2022) for MWoZ - under FT-random and FT-vote-k.
key_metrics: Accuracy for classification and multiple-choice; joint accuracy (Budzianowski et al. 2018) for MWoZ dialogue state tracking; test-suite accuracy (Zhong et al. 2020) for GeoQuery; exact match (Rajpurkar et al. 2016) for NQ; ROUGE-L (Lin 2004) for XSUM. Aggregate reporting uses average absolute gain and relative gain over random selection; stability via min/max across 3 trials.
headline_result: Averaged over 10 datasets, vote-k selective annotation beats random selection by +5.2 absolute / +11.4% relative at an annotation budget of 100, and by +5.8 absolute / +12.9% relative at budget 18 (where no prompt retrieval is needed). In-context learning with only 18 vote-k-selected examples beats 100 randomly selected examples on 6/10 tasks, and matches strong supervised finetuning with 10-100x less annotation cost (e.g. finetuning needs ~1000 examples on HellaSwag and ~800 on MWoZ to match vote-k at 18-100).
ablations: 1) Main Table 2: vote-k vs random at L=18 and L=100 across all 10 datasets (consistent gains, e.g. MRPC 63.5->70.7, SST-5 44.2->53.0, MNLI 37.4->47.3, HellaSwag 65.2->70.7, MWoZ 47.2->51.4 at L=100). 2) ICL vs finetuning (4.1, Fig.2): ICL-vote-k > finetuning of SOTA PLMs; selective annotation helps ICL but NOT finetuning (consistent with active-learning-vs-finetuning literature), attributed to outliers/instability; Appendix E/Table 9 shows removing 10% outliers lets finetuning benefit from vote-k. 3) Model size (4.2, Fig.3): gains larger for smaller models (HellaSwag: +7.5 with GPT-Neo 2.7B vs +2.6 with GPT-3), but consistent across GPT-Neo/GPT-J/GPT-3/OPT-175B. 4) Domain shift (4.3, Table 3, WILDS): vote-k gain larger under domain splits (CivilComments +9.9 domain vs +5.5 random; Amazon +8.3 domain vs +6.0 random). 5) Random prompt retrieval (4.4, Table 4): with random (not similarity) retrieval, vote-k no longer beats random selection (HellaSwag 62.5 vs 63.2) - selection + similarity retrieval are jointly necessary. 6) Alternative selection methods (4.5, Table 5): vote-k > Fast vote-k > Least-confidence/Diversity > MFL > Random (e.g. HellaSwag 70.7 vote-k vs 65.2 random; Fast vote-k 69.5 with 10x+ speedup). 7) Diversity/representativeness analysis (Appendix F, Table 10): vote-k selected sets score higher on DIV-I, DIV-F, and REPR. than random.
evaluation_decoupling: No: only end-to-end downstream task metrics are reported (accuracy / joint accuracy / test-suite accuracy / EM / ROUGE-L). No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG). The closest decoupled diagnostics are the diversity/representativeness measurements of the SELECTED pool (Appendix F), not retrieval recall.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome (final task accuracy/score). Process-style diagnostics are added: stability (min/max over 3 unlabeled subsamples), diversity/representativeness scores of selected sets, and the random-vs-similar retrieval decomposition, but these characterize the selection/retrieval pipeline rather than scoring intermediate reasoning steps.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Annotation efficiency is the central thesis: vote-k matches SOTA finetuning with 10-100x less annotation (e.g. finetuning needs ~800-1000 labels to match vote-k at 18-100); 18 vote-k examples beat 100 random examples on 6/10 tasks. Compute trade-off: full vote-k runs the inference LM over all unlabeled instances to compute confidence (expensive); 'Fast vote-k' drops this for a 10x+ speedup with near-identical accuracy. Test-time retrieval is a single cheap Sentence-BERT nearest-neighbor lookup; on average 13.4 demonstrations are fed per prompt. No explicit dollar/latency numbers; GPT-J 6B is the default ICL model for budget reasons, Codex-davinci-002 for MWoZ/GeoQuery/NQ.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Two budgets. (a) Annotation budget M (the labeled pool size): main experiments use M in {18, 100}; analysis uses {18, 100, 300, 800} (and up to ~1000 for the finetuning comparison). M=18 is chosen because all 18 examples fit in the LM context (no retrieval needed). (b) Prompt context: at M=100, retrieve as many similar examples as fit within the LM's max token length (avg 13.4 in-context examples), ordered ascending by similarity. Vote-k hyperparameters: k=150 nearest neighbors, rho=10 (the discount exponent rho>1 penalizing closeness to already-selected examples); 9M/10 confidence buckets used in the second phase.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (uses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). Selection is performed over a 3K-instance unlabeled subsample of each dataset's training split (resampled 3x for stability); evaluation uses standard test splits where public (SST-5, XSUM, MWoZ, DBpedia) and dev splits otherwise, following prior work.
builds_on: In-context learning / prompt retrieval: Liu et al. 2022 (KATE, similarity-based demonstration retrieval) and Rubin et al. 2022 (EPR, learned prompt retrieval) for the prompt-retrieval step; Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3) for the ICL paradigm. Embeddings: Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019, all-mpnet-base-v2). Selection/active-learning lineage: facility location (Lin & Bilmes 2009), least-confidence active learning (Lewis & Gale 1994). LMs used: GPT-J (Wang & Komatsuzaki 2021), GPT-Neo (Black et al. 2021), GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020), OPT-175B (Zhang et al. 2022), Codex (Chen et al. 2021). Recency-bias ordering from Lu et al. 2022.
contrasts_with: Recent ICL methods that assume a LARGE fully-annotated training set is available for retrieval (Liu et al. 2022 KATE; Rubin et al. 2022 EPR) - this work instead minimizes total annotation cost via a two-step framework. Active-learning / coreset selection baselines for supervised finetuning (facility location/MFL, diversity, least-confidence) - vote-k beats them for ICL, and active learning is shown ineffective for finetuning (Karamcheti et al. 2021; D'Arcy & Downey 2022). Supervised finetuning of strong PLMs (RoBERTa-large, DS2-T5) - ICL-vote-k matches/beats them at far lower annotation cost. Random selection and random prompt retrieval.
lineage: Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). A foundational 2022/ICLR-2023 work that reframes demonstration retrieval around ANNOTATION EFFICIENCY: it adds an upstream unsupervised graph-based selective-annotation stage (vote-k) before the now-standard similarity-based prompt retrieval (KATE/EPR), establishing the select-pool-then-retrieve paradigm. Sits between unsupervised similarity retrieval (KATE) and learned demonstration retrievers (EPR, CEIL, UDR, LLM-R), and connects ICL demonstration selection to the active-learning/coreset-selection literature.
